items.stem: Explain the process of transport of oxygenated and deoxygenated blood in a human body.
items.answer: Pulmonary circulation transports oxygen-poor (deoxygenated) blood from the right ventricle to the lungs, where the blood picks up a fresh supply of oxygen. It then returns the oxygen-rich blood to the left atrium. Systemic circulation carries oxygenated blood from the left ventricle, through the arteries, to the capillaries in the tissues of the body. From the tissue capillaries the deoxygenated blood returns through a system of veins to the right atrium of the heart.

items.stem:
(a) In the process of respiration, state the function of alveoli.
(b) Rate of breathing in aquatic organisms is much faster than that in terrestrial organisms. Give reasons.
(c) Complete the following pathway showing the breakdown of glucose:
Glucose in cytoplasm (6-carbon molecule) → (i) ? (3-carbon molecule) + energy —[Presence of O₂, in mitochondria]→ (ii) ? + H₂O + energy
items.answer:
(a) Function of alveoli: (i) Gaseous exchange takes place in the alveoli in the lungs. (ii) Alveoli provide a large surface area for the exchange of gases.
(b) Terrestrial organisms breathe the oxygen present in the atmosphere, but aquatic organisms use the oxygen dissolved in water. Since the amount of dissolved oxygen in water is very low compared with the amount of oxygen in air (21%), the rate of breathing in aquatic organisms is much faster than in terrestrial organisms.
(c) Glucose in cytoplasm (6-carbon molecule) → (i) Pyruvate (3-carbon molecule) + energy —[Presence of O₂, in mitochondria]→ (ii) CO₂ (carbon dioxide) + H₂O + energy.

items.stem: Mention the three kinds of cells present in blood. Write one function of each.
items.answer:
Blood is made up of plasma and corpuscles. The three kinds of corpuscles are RBC, WBC and blood platelets.
(i) Red blood corpuscles (RBC) are small biconcave cells that contain haemoglobin, which transports O₂ from the lungs to the body cells and CO₂ from the body cells to the lungs.
(ii) White blood cells (WBC) — their main function is defence of the body against diseases and other infections.
(iii) Blood platelets are responsible for the clotting of blood during injuries.

items.stem:
Write one function of each of the following components of the transport system in human beings:
(a) Blood vessels (b) Lymph (c) Heart
items.answer:
(a) Blood vessels: There are three types of blood vessels of different sizes involved in blood circulation, viz. arteries, veins and capillaries, which are all connected into a continuous closed system that carries blood to and from every part of the body.
(b) Lymph: It carries digested and absorbed fat from the intestine and drains excess fluid from the extracellular space back into the blood.
(c) Heart: It is a pumping organ that receives blood from the veins and pumps it into the arteries.

items.stem:
State the functions of the following in the alimentary canal:
(i) Liver (ii) Gall bladder (iii) Villi
items.answer:
(i) Liver: (a) It secretes bile juice. (b) Bile salts break down large globules of fat into smaller globules to increase the efficiency of enzyme action.
(ii) Gall bladder: (a) It stores the bile secreted by the liver. (b) The bile from the gall bladder is transported to the small intestine through the bile duct.
(iii) Villi: (a) They are finger-like projections found on the inner wall of the small intestine. (b) They greatly increase the absorptive surface area of the inner lining of the intestine for the absorption of digested food.

items.answer:

(b) It is the site of the complete digestion of carbohydrates, proteins and fats.
(c) The secretions of the liver and the pancreas are released into this part.

(e) Bile salts break down large globules of fat into smaller globules, increasing the efficiency of enzyme action.

(ii) The amino acids are absorbed by the blood and transported through the blood vessels to the cells and tissues.
(iii) In the cells, the amino acids are used up for building the components of cells and tissues. These are the basic materials for growth.

items.stem:
(a) Blood pressure is high in the arteries and low in the veins. Give the possible reason for such a difference.
(b) What is the major cause of high blood pressure?
(c) What may happen if a person is having a very high blood pressure?
items.answer:
(a) Blood pressure is the force that blood exerts against the walls of the vessels by the discharge of blood into them by the contraction of the left ventricle. The heart pushes blood into the arteries under great force, and this pressure gradually drops as blood travels onward. Therefore, blood pressure is high in the arteries and capillaries and finally becomes very low in the veins.
(b) High blood pressure is caused by the constriction of the arterioles.
(c) Constriction of the arterioles results in increased resistance to blood flow, leading to the rupture of an artery and internal bleeding.

items.stem: Why is respiration important for all living organisms?
items.answer:
Respiration is important for all living organisms because:
(i) For obtaining energy: the oxygen which we inhale along with air oxidises the food and liberates energy.
(ii) For the removal of toxic carbon dioxide: carbon dioxide is produced in our tissues as a result of the oxidation of food. CO₂ is injurious to our body if it accumulates in the tissues in higher concentration and for a longer period. During respiration, gaseous exchange (O₂ and CO₂) takes place between the tissue and the blood. During this process CO₂ from the tissues gets diffused into the blood. The blood takes this CO₂ to the respiratory organs (e.g. the lungs), from where it is eliminated back into the atmosphere.

items.stem: What are the various steps involved in the holozoic mode of nutrition?
items.answer:
The different steps of the holozoic mode of nutrition are (i) Ingestion (ii) Digestion (iii) Absorption (iv) Assimilation (v) Egestion.
Ingestion is the taking in of food into the body or alimentary canal. Amoeba engulfs the food by forming pseudopodia all around it and captures the food into a food vacuole; this is called phagocytosis.
Digestion is the breaking down of complex and insoluble food with the help of enzymes into simpler and soluble substances so that they can be utilised in the body. In Amoeba digestion occurs in the food vacuole with the help of digestive enzymes.
Absorption is the diffusion of the digested food into the cytoplasm.
Assimilation is the utilisation of the digested food by the cell.
Egestion is the removal or throwing out of the undigested food from the body.

items.stem: How do the guard cells regulate the opening and closing of stomatal pores? Explain with the help of a diagram. Also indicate what happens to the rate of photosynthesis if the stomata get blocked due to dust.
items.answer: The swelling of the guard cells due to the absorption of water causes the opening of the stomatal pore, while the shrinking of the guard cells closes the pore. The rate of photosynthesis decreases when the stomata of a leaf get blocked due to dust, because the entry of CO₂ is reduced.

items.stem: Describe an experiment to prove that CO₂ is necessary for photosynthesis.
items.answer: Take two healthy potted plants which are nearly of the same size. Keep them in a dark room for three days. Place a watch-glass containing potassium hydroxide by the side of one of the plants; the potassium hydroxide is used to absorb carbon dioxide. Cover both plants with separate bell jars. Use vaseline to seal the bottom of the jars to the glass plates so that the set-up is air-tight. Keep the plants in sunlight for about two hours. Pluck a leaf from each plant and test it for the presence of starch. The leaf from the plant near which potassium hydroxide was not placed shows the presence of starch, while the other does not. This experiment shows that CO₂ is necessary for photosynthesis.

items.stem: Explain the mechanism of breathing.
items.answer:
For continued gaseous exchange in the lungs a constant renewal of air is necessary. This happens in two steps.
(i) Inspiration (inhalation), i.e. drawing air into the lungs, is the result of an increase in the size of the thoracic cavity due to the combined action of the ribs and the diaphragm. The ribs are moved upward and outward by the intercostal muscles, enlarging the chest cavity all around. The diaphragm, a sheet of muscular tissue normally arched upward like a dome towards the base of the lungs, contracts and flattens to an almost horizontal plane, enlarging the chest cavity lengthwise. As the chest cavity increases in size the pressure inside the lungs falls below atmospheric pressure, so outside air rushes in to equalise the pressure.
(ii) Expiration (exhalation), i.e. expelling air out, is the result of the reverse movements of the ribs and the diaphragm. The other set of intercostal muscles contracts and pulls the ribs down and inward, and the diaphragm relaxes and moves upward to its dome-like outline under the pressure of the abdominal contents. The cavity of the thorax is diminished, the lungs are compressed and the air is forced out into the atmosphere.

items.stem: Write down the functions of the blood.
items.answer:
The different functions of blood are:
(i) Transport of nutrients.
(ii) Transport of respiratory gases (O₂ and CO₂).
(iii) Transport of metabolic waste products (urea, uric acid, ammonia, etc.).
(iv) Transport of enzymes and hormones.
(v) Transport of ions.

items.stem:
What is the composition of blood? Give one function of each of its components.
OR
Name the constituents of blood.
items.answer:
Blood is a liquid connective tissue. It chiefly contains two components:
(i) Fluid matrix or plasma, which is colourless and transports many substances like glucose, amino acids, urea, etc. It contains a lot of water and many proteins.
(ii) Cellular elements, which are of three types: (a) Red blood corpuscles (RBCs) or erythrocytes, which transport O₂ and CO₂; (b) White blood corpuscles (WBCs) or leucocytes, which fight disease-causing agents; (c) Blood platelets or thrombocytes, which help in blood clotting.

items.stem:
(a) Draw a neat diagram of the respiratory system and label the following parts: (i) Lungs (ii) Trachea (iii) Bronchus (iv) Diaphragm.
(b) Name the respiratory pigment in human beings and discuss its role.
(c) Why is the rate of breathing in aquatic organisms much faster than that in terrestrial organisms?
items.answer:
(a) The labelled diagram of the respiratory system should mark the lungs, the trachea, the bronchus and the diaphragm.
(b) Haemoglobin is the respiratory pigment in human beings. It takes up O₂ from the air in the lungs and carries it to the tissues that are deficient in oxygen.
(c) The amount of dissolved oxygen in water is fairly low compared with the amount of oxygen in air, so aquatic organisms have to breathe much faster than terrestrial organisms.

items.stem: Briefly describe the shape and function of human red blood corpuscles.
items.answer: RBCs are circular, biconcave discs and do not contain nuclei. An RBC contains a respiratory pigment called haemoglobin; it is because of this pigment that the blood appears red. Haemoglobin carries oxygen from the lungs to the tissues and carbon dioxide from the tissues to the lungs. The lifespan of an RBC is about 120 days.

items.stem:
(i) Draw a sectional view of the human heart and label: (a) Pulmonary artery (b) Aorta (c) Septum (d) Ventricles.
(ii) Arteries have thick elastic walls while veins have valves. Explain.
items.answer:
(i) The sectional view of the human heart is drawn with the pulmonary artery, the aorta, the septum and the ventricles labelled on it.
(ii) Arteries carry blood at a lot of pressure, so they need thick elastic walls, whereas veins carry blood at low pressure and therefore have valves to prevent the back flow of blood.
